FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Kids Games flashcards.

Every classic game a childhood needs, on twenty-six cards a kid can read. Each card names one game — the balloon you keep off the floor, the potato that burns hands, the bear-hug hide-and-seek behind the bush — and each card page carries a simple guide: what you need, how to play, and one way to make it fresh tomorrow. The games speak the everyday words of the US, UK and Canada — and where the countries differ (tic-tac-toe and noughts and crosses, jump rope and skipping rope, freeze dance and musical statues), both names ride along, so every family hears its own playground talking.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Game Day draw

    Stack the cards face down, draw one, read its guide together and play. The winner of each game draws the next card — the afternoon runs itself, and the stack decides everything.

  2. 02

    Same game, two names

    The cards quietly carry both flavors of English: tic-tac-toe and noughts and crosses, jump rope and skipping rope, freeze dance and musical statues. Say both — your child picks a favorite, or keeps both like secrets.

  3. 03

    Losing practice

    Games are the gentlest teacher of losing there is. Play short rounds, cheer the winner loudly, and say "good game!" — the rematch matters more than the trophy.

  4. 04

    The rainy-day shelf

    Keep the five sit-down cards (bingo, memory, tic-tac-toe, maze, puzzle) in a basket near the couch. On a gray afternoon the basket is the plan.

  5. 05

    One rule, retold

    Before every game, ask your child to say the one rule out loud — "keep it up!", "freeze when the music stops!". A child who can say the rule can run the game with friends.

      Balloon Keep-Up Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Throw, roll & aim

      Balloon keep-up is the one rule everyone knows before you say it: the balloon must never touch the floor. Tap it up, chase it, tap it again — the balloon falls slowly enough that even the littlest player gets a real turn at saving it.

      Say it together

      “Balloon keep-up! The balloon is sleepy and wants to fall — tap it gently to wake it up. One tap, two taps — do not let it touch the floor!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Count the taps out loud: how many saves before it lands? Tomorrow, try the harder way — one hand only, or everyone sits on the floor and the balloon may never go higher than your head.

      Quick parent note

      A blown-up balloon falls slowly, which is exactly why this game works for threes: it gives slow children time and fast children a real challenge. UK playgrounds call this style of game keepy-uppy — same game, another name.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Balloon Keep-Up lesson on the Learning Path.

      Beanbag Toss Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Throw, roll & aim

      Beanbag toss is an aiming game with a soft, forgiving star: the beanbag. Step back, aim at the target holes and let it fly — a beanbag that misses does not bounce away or hurt anything, so throwing hard and missing stays fun.

      Say it together

      “Beanbag toss! Hold it flat in your hand, look at the hole, step forward and — throw! Did it land in? A beanbag on the floor still counts as a practice throw.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Start close and step back one heel-toe step after every success. Three in the middle hole earns a cheer; three misses in a row means you move closer instead — the game bends to the thrower.

      Quick parent note

      A beanbag is the best first throwing object because it lands and stays. No beanbag? A rolled-up sock is a perfectly honest beanbag — every family owns the equipment already.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Beanbag Toss lesson on the Learning Path.

      Bowling Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Throw, roll & aim

      Bowling is the rolling game: line up the pins, stand back, and roll the ball along the floor so it knocks as many as it can. Ten pins is the real set, but three cups or bottles make a perfectly good alley in any hallway.

      Say it together

      “Bowling! The pins are standing in a triangle. Roll the ball low and slow — rrroll — and down they go! Count how many fell, then stand them up again.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Set the pins up together — that is half the game. Take turns: one roll each, count the fallen pins out loud, and the fell-then-standing rhythm keeps everyone busy even while waiting.

      Quick parent note

      Rolling is a skill younger children learn faster than throwing, and hallway bowling needs no equipment beyond a soft ball and three empty bottles. The counting after each roll is real math practice wearing a bowling shirt.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bowling lesson on the Learning Path.

      Hoop Toss Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Throw, roll & aim

      Hoop toss is carnival arithmetic: throw the rings at the pegs and land one around a post. The rings marked closest score little, the far ones score a lot — 10, 20, 30, 50 — so every throw is also a small decision.

      Say it together

      “Hoop toss! Hold the ring flat like a frisbee, look at the peg, and let it fly. Ten points if it lands near, fifty if you ring the far one!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Keep score with a tally on paper — a mark for every ten. Five rounds each, then add the tallies together and crown the ring champion (and offer a rematch immediately, as tradition demands).

      Quick parent note

      Scoring games like this quietly teach that numbers can be worth different amounts, and adding tallies is the friendliest first math there is. Rings that miss simply lie on the grass waiting to be gathered — gathering is part of the turn.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Hoop Toss lesson on the Learning Path.

      Paper Plane Target Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Throw, roll & aim

      Paper plane target is two games folded into one: first you fold the plane (the craft half), then you throw it at a target (the aim half). A drawn bullseye on the floor — or a laundry basket — becomes the landing zone every flight dreams about.

      Say it together

      “Paper plane target! Fold the plane, stand behind the line, and let it fly at the bullseye. Did it land close? One point. Did it land in the circle? Three points!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Fold two planes and race them — the winner is whichever lands nearest the target. Try throwing soft, then hard, and discover which way flies straighter. Every flight teaches the next fold.

      Quick parent note

      In the UK the same toy is a paper aeroplane — same folds, different word. Folding is the real skill here; a four-year-old who can make the first two folds is doing honest origami with a job at the end.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Paper Plane Target lesson on the Learning Path.

      Duck, Duck, Goose Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Run, chase & freeze

      Duck, duck, goose is the circle game every birthday party runs on. Everyone sits in a ring; one child walks around tapping heads saying "duck... duck... GOOSE!" — and the goose leaps up and chases the tapper once around the circle.

      Say it together

      “Duck, duck, duck... GOOSE! Run around the ring and back to the empty spot before the goose catches you! Sit down fast — the goose is quick today.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play with the gentle rule that the tapper walks and the goose runs. After a few rounds, let your child be the tapper — choosing who to pick is the secret, delicious power of this game.

      Quick parent note

      This is the classic game for practicing wait-and-go: sitting children must hold still, and the goose must explode into running at one exact word. Three or more players is enough; a soft floor helps everyone fall more kindly.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Duck, Duck, Goose lesson on the Learning Path.

      Follow the Leader Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Run, chase & freeze

      Follow the leader is a copying game with a moving classroom: one child leads and does anything at all — hopping, tiptoeing, waving, going silly — and everyone behind copies every single move. Then the leader hands the crown to the next player.

      Say it together

      “Follow the leader! March, march — now hop! Now tiptoe like a mouse — shh! Everybody copies the leader, and when I say "new leader", it is someone else’s turn to decide the moves.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Take the leader job yourself first and make the moves easy to copy: touch your nose, spin once, walk backward. Then hand the crown over. A quiet child often leads loudest on round two.

      Quick parent note

      Copying movement is real body-brain work — watching, understanding and matching at speed. Swap leaders every minute or so; the rotation keeps the game moving faster than the boredom can arrive.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Follow the Leader lesson on the Learning Path.

      Freeze Dance Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Run, chase & freeze

      Freeze dance is dancing with one giant button: when the music plays, everybody dances their silliest; when the music stops, everybody freezes like statues. Wiggle one finger too late and you are (kindly) out for one round.

      Say it together

      “Freeze dance! When the music plays — dance, dance, dance! When it stops — FREEZE! Like a statue, like a robot, like a snowman. Nobody move... hold it... hold it...”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play DJ yourself: stop the music at silly moments, mid-jump if you can. The frozen poses themselves become the show — take a picture of the best statue and let the statue see it after.

      Quick parent note

      American families say freeze dance; British families often say musical statues — same game, two shores. Stopping your own body on a signal is a real self-control skill, and this is the only game where practicing it feels like a party.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Freeze Dance lesson on the Learning Path.

      Hide and Seek Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Run, chase & freeze

      Hide and seek is the oldest game in the world and still the best. The seeker closes their eyes and counts to ten out loud; everybody else melts into hiding spots; then the seeking begins — and being found is half the fun.

      Say it together

      “Hide and seek! One... two... three... (loud, so the hiders can hear) ...nine, TEN! Ready or not, here I come! I wonder where everybody is hiding...”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      For threes, hide together at first — you and your child in one spot, giggling, while a grown-up seeks. Teach the house rules kindly: no hiding where doors close, and the curtain behind the sofa always counts.

      Quick parent note

      Counting out loud is the game’s built-in math lesson, and the seeking is a real memory test — where WERE they last time? Agree the safe zones before round one: hiders stay where a grown-up can find them in one look.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Hide and Seek lesson on the Learning Path.

      Hot Potato Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Run, chase & freeze

      Hot potato is a passing game played at comedy speed: everyone sits in a circle and passes the potato (a ball, a beanbag, a real potato) from hand to hand while the music plays. When the music stops — the one holding it is the funny, harmless loser of the round.

      Say it together

      “Hot potato! Pass it quick, pass it quick — the potato is HOT! Do not hold it, throw it — no wait, pass it gently — quick quick! ...Music stopped! Who has the potato?”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pass left to start, then try passing right. Speed the music up and the potato gets hotter. The holder of the stopped potato does one funny task — hop three times — and the game rolls on.

      Quick parent note

      Fast passing is a handover skill hiding inside a party game, and the "loser" rule here is the gentlest one ever invented: you hold a pretend-hot potato, you hop like a frog, everyone laughs WITH you. Keep the potato soft and the music short.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Hot Potato lesson on the Learning Path.

      Musical Chairs Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Run, chase & freeze

      Musical chairs is the walking-freezing game with furniture: chairs in a circle, one fewer chair than players, music on and everybody walks. When the music stops — sit! The player left standing sits out a round and cheers loudly from the sidelines.

      Say it together

      “Musical chairs! Walk around the circle — walking feet only, no running — when the music stops, find a chair and SIT! One chair goes away each round... here comes the music...”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      For threes, play the kind version: two chairs for the last two players and a shared win, or the left-standing player becomes the DJ who stops the music next round. The job is better than the chair.

      Quick parent note

      Walking-not-running is the rule that makes this game safe in a living room — say it every round like a referee. Losing a chair kindly, then getting a new job, is the emotional lesson hiding under all the noise.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Musical Chairs lesson on the Learning Path.

      Red Light, Green Light Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Run, chase & freeze

      Red light, green light turns a living room or a yard into a traffic school. The caller stands at one end; the players line up at the other. "Green light!" means run forward; "red light!" means freeze on the spot. First one to reach the caller wins the flashlight for the next round.

      Say it together

      “Red light, green light! When I say GREEN LIGHT — run! When I say RED LIGHT — stop like a statue! Green light... RED LIGHT! Nobody move! ...Green light!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Let your child take the caller job — calling the lights is the best seat in the game. Trick rounds make it comedy: call "red light" in your green voice, and catch every wiggler.

      Quick parent note

      Stopping on a word is a whole safety lesson dressed as a game — this is how children practice "stop" with their whole bodies. Any distance works: three meters of hallway is a full game; a whole yard is a championship.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Red Light, Green Light lesson on the Learning Path.

      Bingo Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Table & take turns

      Bingo is the matching game with a winner shout: every player holds a card of pictures, a caller picks and names them one by one, and players cover the ones on their card. First to fill a whole row shouts BINGO! — the loudest word in table games.

      Say it together

      “Bingo! Look at your card. I call the picture — you find it and cover it! A star... a duck... who has a duck? ...Every square in one row covered? Shout BINGO!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      For first games use picture bingo (the card art does the reading) and call slowly, naming each picture twice. Let your child be the caller for one round — being the voice at the table is its own kind of winning.

      Quick parent note

      Bingo quietly drills matching, listening and taking turns at once. Small winning tweaks for threes: two-in-a-row wins, or every completed square gets a count. The B-I-N-G-O letters on real cards are bonus letter practice for the fours.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bingo lesson on the Learning Path.

      Fishing Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Table & take turns

      The fishing game is a pond in your living room: paper fish with paper-clip mouths swim on the floor, and each player holds a rod with a magnet on the string. Dangle, wait, and — GOT ONE! — the fish leaps off the floor and into your bucket.

      Say it together

      “Fishing time! Hold the rod steady... let the line dangle... wait for it... GOT ONE! You caught the pink fish! Put it in your bucket and pass the rod to the next fisher.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make the fish from paper, clip a paper clip on each nose, and tie a magnet to a stick on a string. Count the catch at the end — who caught the most, and who caught the biggest (that one weighs nothing and wins anyway).

      Quick parent note

      Steady hands and patience are the whole lesson — the magnet does not hurry, and neither can the fisher. Taking turns with one rod teaches waiting better than any timer; two rods doubles the pond fun if waiting gets wobbly.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Fishing lesson on the Learning Path.

      Four in a Row Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Table & take turns

      Four in a row is the dropping-discs game where a grid fills from the bottom up: take turns dropping your colored discs into the columns, and the first to line up four of their own — across, up or on the slant — wins. The boxed version many families know is called Connect Four.

      Say it together

      “Four in a row! Drop your disc in — clunk! — and I drop mine. Look out: if I get four in a line, I win! Watch the rows AND the slopes — four can hide on an angle.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      First games, play open-book style: point out threats out loud ("uh oh, you have three in a row!") so blocking becomes the game. Once blocking clicks, stop helping and let the strategies go secret.

      Quick parent note

      This is often a child’s first strategy game — the grid shows every possibility at once, so planning is visible. It is sold in stores as Connect Four, but a drawn grid and two colors of buttons or cereal pieces play the exact same game.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Four in a Row lesson on the Learning Path.

      Memory Match Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Table & take turns

      Memory match is the flipping game with a remembering brain at its heart: all the cards lie face down, and on your turn you turn over two. A matching pair is yours to keep; a miss goes back face down — and everyone tries to remember where it lives.

      Say it together

      “Memory match! Turn one card... now a second. An apple and an apple — a pair! You keep them! Two different ones? Turn them back and remember where they were...”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Start with just six cards (three pairs) face down — small grids make young memories feel mighty. Grow the grid as the finding gets faster. The proud moment to listen for: "I KNEW where that one was!"

      Quick parent note

      In the UK this game is often simply called pairs — same cards, shorter name. Memory games are honest brain training for everyone at the table, and grown-ups lose honestly to four-year-olds more often than they admit.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Memory Match lesson on the Learning Path.

      Rock, Paper, Scissors Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Table & take turns

      Rock, paper, scissors is the two-second decision game the whole world agrees on: fist bumps on "scissors, shoot!" and out come the hands — rock blunts scissors, scissors cut paper, paper wraps rock. It settles who goes first in every other game ever invented.

      Say it together

      “Rock, paper, scissors — shoot! Make your hand at the same time: a fist is rock, a flat hand is paper, two fingers are scissors. Rock breaks scissors... scissors cut paper... paper covers rock!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Chant together — "rock, paper, scissors, SHOOT" — the shoot is when hands appear. Best of three makes a fair referee. Then use it the way the playground does: to decide who goes first at everything, all day long.

      Quick parent note

      The hand signs are a fine-motor workout hiding in a fist fight: fist, flat, two fingers, fast. It is also the fairest referee ever invented — no arguing with the hands, and the loser learns to lose in two seconds flat.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Rock, Paper, Scissors lesson on the Learning Path.

      Tic-Tac-Toe Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Table & take turns

      Tic-tac-toe is the first strategy game most children ever master: a nine-square grid, X and O, alternating turns — and the first player to get three of their marks in a row (across, down or on the diagonal) draws the winning line. In the UK the same game is called noughts and crosses.

      Say it together

      “Tic-tac-toe! You are X and I am O. Put your X in a square — now I put my O somewhere. Three of yours in a row? You win! Three of mine? I win! Watch the diagonals — they are sneaky.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Draw the grid on paper, or chalk it on the sidewalk and play with rocks and leaves. Teach the block openly at first ("if I get two here, you must go THERE") — then play five quiet rounds and let the strategies become theirs.

      Quick parent note

      British families say noughts and crosses — nought is the round zero, cross is the X. The deep secret children discover eventually: smart players can always force a draw, and a drawn game between two careful players is a victory of thinking.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Tic-Tac-Toe lesson on the Learning Path.

      Maze Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Look, find & solve

      A maze is a puzzle you solve with your eyes and one brave finger: find the entrance marked START, travel the winding paths, and reach the FINISH star without crossing a wall. Wrong turns are part of the fun — every dead end teaches the map.

      Say it together

      “Maze time! Put your finger on START... go slowly... this way... oops, a dead end! Back up and try the other path... there is the FINISH star! You did it!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Trace with a finger first, then with a pencil once the route is known. Make your own maze for someone else — a few wrong paths drawn on purpose is half the art. Trade mazes and solve each other’s.

      Quick parent note

      Mazes train the quiet skills: looking ahead, holding a plan, and calmly backing up from a dead end — which is resilience practice disguised as a puzzle. Finger-tracing is a real pre-writing exercise; the pencil just makes it official.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Puzzle Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Look, find & solve

      A puzzle is a picture broken into promises: every piece has exactly one home, and your job is to find it. Corners first, edges next, colors and shapes as clues — and that last piece is the best feeling in quiet games.

      Say it together

      “Puzzle time! Look at the picture on the box. Find a piece with a flat edge — that is the border! Does this piece fit here? Turn it... try it... click! It belongs!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sort pieces into piles before starting: edge pieces, colors, "the ones with the tree". Help for thirty seconds, then hands off — the pride of a finished puzzle only works if the hands doing it are small.

      Quick parent note

      Puzzles are shape-rotation practice — turning a piece in the mind until it fits — plus the patience to try, fail and try again without anyone losing. Start with twelve big pieces; the jump to twenty-four is a real graduation.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Spot the Difference Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Look, find & solve

      Spot the difference is two almost-twin pictures side by side — and something is different. A cloud missing, a door colored blue instead of red, a tree that walked away. Look slowly, back and forth, and point when you find a change.

      Say it together

      “Spot the difference! Look at the two houses. Same same same... but WAIT — what is different? Look at the sky... look at the trees... count them! How many changes are hiding?”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play detective: point at each change and say it out loud — "this picture has an extra cloud!" Take turns finding one each. Make your own pair later: draw a simple scene, then copy it with one sneaky change.

      Quick parent note

      Comparing two pictures side by side is honest visual training — the eyes learn to sweep, hold and compare, the same motion reading will need. Four-year-olds are magnificent at this game; grown-ups are reliably worse and should lose gracefully.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Treasure Hunt Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Look, find & solve

      A treasure hunt turns your whole home into a map: clues lead from one spot to the next ("look under the red cushion"), each clue points to the next, and the trail ends at the treasure — a snack, a sticker, a shiny stone from the garden.

      Say it together

      “Treasure hunt! Here is the first clue: go to the place where we keep the cold milk... the fridge! Look inside — another clue! Follow the trail, clue by clue, until you find the treasure!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Five clues is a full adventure. Draw simple pictures as clues for pre-readers (a picture of the bookshelf). The treasure matters less than the trail — a single cookie at the end of five clues tastes like gold.

      Quick parent note

      A hunt teaches following directions in order — the skill behind every recipe and every school instruction. Hide the treasure BEFORE bedtime and the game runs itself while you drink your coffee. X marks the spot; your sofa cushions mark everything else.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Treasure Hunt lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Charades Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Act, guess & listen

      Charades is acting with a silence rule: draw a card or whisper an animal or an action, then act it out — hopping like a bunny, stirring like a chef, roaring like a lion — without saying a word, while everyone else shouts guesses.

      Say it together

      “Charades! I will act like something and you guess what I am. No words from me — only moving! (hop hop hop) What am I? A bunny! Your turn — act like something big...”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Start with animals — they have the clearest movements. Then try actions: brushing teeth, sleeping, kicking a ball. The actor points at guesses to say "warmer" (thumbs up) or "colder" (thumbs down).

      Quick parent note

      Acting without words is imagination plus body control plus reading an audience — a whole theater degree in a party game. Guesses should be kind and silly in equal measure; the best rounds end with everyone acting at once.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Charades lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Simon Says Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 3+Act, guess & listen

      Simon says is the listening game with a trick built in: when the leader says "Simon says touch your toes" — touch your toes! But if the leader only says "touch your toes"... do NOT move. The trap is the game, and catching yourself is the fun.

      Say it together

      “Simon says — touch your nose! Simon says — hop on one foot! Now... touch your toes! (no "Simon says" — did anybody move?) The magic words are SIMON SAYS. Without them, nobody moves!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the leader yourself first, mixing honest commands with three sneaky traps. Then hand over the crown — a child caller learns quickly that the fun is in the trick, not the trap. Fast rounds, big laughs, nobody really out.

      Quick parent note

      This is the purest listening game ever invented: it trains catching the exact words, holding an instruction in mind, and stopping an impulse — the full attention toolkit. Keep rounds short and let the "out" players rejoin next round; the game is the listening, not the elimination.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Hopscotch Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Playground & outdoors

      Hopscotch is chalk, sidewalk and hopping: draw the numbered course, throw a small stone onto a square, then hop the course — one foot on singles, two feet on the side-by-side pairs — turn at the top and hop back, collecting your stone on the way.

      Say it together

      “Hopscotch! Throw the stone onto a number — it landed on 4! Now hop the squares: one foot, one foot, two feet, two feet... jump OVER square 4, turn at the top, and hop back to pick it up!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Draw the course with chalk — numbering the squares 1 to 10 is the first job and the first math. Too hard to hop one-footed? Hop two-footed through the whole course; the course bends to the hopper.

      Quick parent note

      Hopscotch is number order, balance and turn-taking drawn on the ground — the sidewalk is the worksheet. It is played on every continent under almost every name; the chalk wears out long before the game does.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Jump Rope Flashcard for Kids

      Ages 4–5Playground & outdoors

      Jump rope is a swing, a jump and a rhythm: turn the rope overhead, let it sweep the ground toward your feet, and hop over it — once, twice, then as many as the rhythm allows. Two players can swing while one jumps, and the chants do the counting.

      Say it together

      “Jump rope! Swing it over — whoosh — and jump as it comes down! One jump! Again — two jumps! Two friends can turn the rope and chant while you jump: "jack be nimble, jack be quick..."”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      First steps without the rope: jump in place to a count. Then hold one handle yourself while a grown-up swings the other side. The double-jump rhythm (rope and feet together) arrives on its own after a dozen tries — celebrate every one.

      Quick parent note

      In the UK the same rope is a skipping rope and the game is skipping — same swing, same songs. Jumping rope is balance, rhythm and burst-power in one toy that costs almost nothing; the songs are the whole culture of the playground riding along.

      Teach it, step by step
